queries: i just potted my alocasia babies last week, how much light do they need

chunks.content: Once past acclimation, all of these aroids, and variegated forms especially, want a lot of light. Grow lights here sit very close to the plants and run twelve to fourteen hours a day, with the plants getting at least 250 PPFD and ideally 300 or more. Acclimating plantlets use a lower target of around 150 PPFD; see the acclimation protocol.

chunks.content: All established plants get at least 12 hours of light a day. Acclimating plantlets get 10 to 12, sometimes 12. The schedule is never shortened.
chunks.heading: Photoperiod used here

chunks.content: Big-box labels call tropical aroids medium- or low-light plants. Indoors, they almost never are. These are not outdoor plants unless they are slowly acclimated to sun, but as indoor plants they need more light than people think. Every aroid grown here is treated as a high-light plant with a target DLI of 15 or more, and established plants are given at least 250 PPFD, with 300 or more as the goal. Tissue-culture plantlets start lower, around 150 PPFD (it is not an exact figure), and pick up more light as they grow toward the fixture.
chunks.heading: Aroids are high-light plants, whatever the store label says

chunks.content: Alocasia are heavy feeders and need a lot of nutrients, plus consistent light. They also need very consistent watering and do not tolerate an irregular schedule the way a Monstera might. A self-watering setup is highly recommended for Alocasia to keep the watering consistent.
chunks.heading: Alocasia need consistent water, fertilizer, and light

chunks.content: Root growth is the main sign. With clear pots, visible roots mean things are going well. A second check when roots are not visible yet: tap the plant lightly, and if it feels more stable in the pot than before, it is rooting. Alocasia can drop every leaf during acclimation and people give up on them, but as long as the center of the plant, the rhizome, is still firm, keep it and keep watering; it will grow back.
chunks.heading: Signs acclimation is working

answer:
Right after potting, treat them as acclimating plantlets: aim for around 150 PPFD (not an exact figure, just the starting target), and they pick up more light as they grow toward the fixture. Run the light 10 to 12 hours a day during this stage, sometimes up to 12 — don't shorten the photoperiod. Once they're past acclimation and rooted in, bump them up to at least 250 PPFD, ideally 300 or more, for 12 to 14 hours a day, since Alocasia (like the other aroids here) are treated as high-light plants indoors regardless of what a store label says.

Alongside light, Alocasia also need very consistent watering and feeding — they don't tolerate an irregular schedule the way a Monstera can, so a self-watering setup is worth considering to keep that consistent.

queries: What should I use as fertilizer?

chunks.content: A varied group of fertilizer products is used here and the brand does not matter. What matters is a 3-1-2 NPK ratio in any multiple: 6-2-4 and 9-3-6 are the same thing. If the fertilizer does not already include calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement. Dosing depends on the specific brand, so follow that product's label rather than a fixed rule; the standing practice is a light dose with every watering except the flush.
chunks.heading: Fertilizer: any 3-1-2 ratio, plus cal-mag

chunks.content: Alongside the IBA rooting hormone and Trichoderma T-22 in the first watering, Big Foot mycorrhizae and a "living charcoal" product are used: a biochar blended with natural fertilizers such as blood meal and worm castings. Exact brands vary and are hard to source consistently, so treat these as the categories to look for rather than specific products to buy.
chunks.heading: Rooting and biological products used here

chunks.content: For the first watering, per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. That very small fertilizer dose in the first watering of the soil has resulted in success. Water the freshly potted plantlets with this once. After that, the next watering gets no fertilizer, and very light feeding starts with the watering after it. Under a 100 percent humidity dome it is usually at least ten days before they need water again.
chunks.heading: What goes in the first watering

chunks.content: Every watering carries a light dose of fertilizer, for all plants (tissue-culture plantlets skip it on their second watering), and this produced a large increase in growth. The other levers for a plant that has stalled are more light and a consistent routine.
chunks.heading: Light fertilizing with every watering

chunks.content: Past the first mix, plants move to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. A very large Alocasia with thick roots can eventually move to a chunkier mix, but that is far in the future.
chunks.heading: Second-stage mix after acclimation: chunky aroid soil

answer:
Use any fertilizer with a 3-1-2 NPK ratio (in any multiple — 6-2-4 and 9-3-6 both count). Brand doesn't matter. If it doesn't already contain calcium and magnesium, add a cal-mag supplement. Dosing depends on the specific product, so follow that brand's label rather than a fixed rule. The standing practice here is a light dose with every watering, except during a flush.

For tissue-culture plantlets specifically: the first watering after potting gets a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer along with a dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone and Trichoderma harzianum T-22, per half liter of water. The next watering after that gets no fertilizer at all. Light feeding then starts with the watering after that, and continues lightly with every watering going forward.

answer:
It depends on the stage and the plant, but here's the pattern.

First mix, right after acclimation: Monstera and Anthurium get about 45 percent tree fern fiber, 45 percent perlite, and 10 percent coco coir. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same base but with about 20 percent coco coir, with tree fern and perlite each dropping a bit to make room. This adds more dense material for their finer roots to pull water from. Any plant with very fine, thin roots should get this denser version, since fine roots need less airflow and need to be able to grab water from the substrate. Going too dense is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

Second mix, once past acclimation: move to a chunky aroid soil made of coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera gets the chunkiest version. Anthurium gets a slightly less chunky version, since their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients but with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle if the mix is too chunky. queries: How long before I should lower humidity on my alocasias?

chunks.content: Alocasia stay at 100 percent humidity for about 15 to 20 days before the step-down starts, longer than a Monstera. Then, instead of reaching 65 percent humidity in about three weeks the way a Monstera does, an Alocasia takes four to five weeks to reach 65 percent. Once acclimated, an Alocasia is still not moved straight into ambient room humidity the way a Monstera can be; to bring one down to ambient humidity, give it a gradual acclimation like the one used for the tissue culture.
chunks.heading: Alocasia need a slower humidity step-down than Monstera

chunks.content: There is no single tell. Acclimation is done when the dome or lid can stay completely off and the plant is ready to move up a pot size. In a grow space held at 65 to 80 percent ambient humidity, stepping a Monstera down from 100 percent to 65 percent takes about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Alocasia take four to five weeks. Anthurium and Philodendron sit in between. A drier room takes longer for all of them.
chunks.heading: When acclimation is done

chunks.content: Monstera are faster growers and more tolerant of problems than Alocasia or Anthurium. A Monstera reaches 65 percent humidity in about three weeks, roughly 18 to 21 days, sometimes a little longer. Once a Monstera is acclimated to 75 to 80 percent humidity and is more than a few inches tall, roughly in a three-inch pot, it can go straight into 50 percent humidity without issues. Alocasia need a much slower step-down and should not be moved like this.
chunks.heading: Monstera tolerate a faster humidity step-down

chunks.content: Alocasia lose leaves during acclimation very often. Most of the time new leaves replace the ones that drop. If the plant goes dormant instead, give it one to two months, sometimes longer, to show signs of growth or improvement before giving up, as long as the rhizome at the center stays firm.
chunks.heading: Leaf drop during Alocasia acclimation is normal

chunks.content: Philodendron sit between Monstera and Alocasia on humidity step-down: more time than a Monstera's three weeks, less than an Alocasia's four to five. They get a little longer than a Monstera specifically because their roots are thinner.
chunks.heading: Philodendron humidity step-down

answer:
Keep your Alocasia at 100 percent humidity for about 15 to 20 days before starting the step-down. After that, the step-down itself is slower than for a Monstera: it takes four to five weeks to reach 65 percent humidity, instead of the roughly three weeks a Monstera takes.

Even once fully acclimated, don't move it straight to ambient room humidity like you could with a Monstera. Bring it down gradually, the same kind of gradual acclimation used when it first came out of tissue culture.

If it drops leaves during this process, that's normal, new leaves usually replace them. If it goes dormant instead, give it one to two months, sometimes longer, to show growth again, as long as the center rhizome stays firm.

queries: whats the best way to deal with thrips on my baby aroids

chunks.content: Spider mites are an easier kill than thrips. Neem oil, spinosad, or most other pesticide sprays work, combined with manually wiping the leaves. Wipe both sides of each leaf.
chunks.heading: Spider mites: sprays plus wiping

chunks.content: Thrips adapt to pesticides quickly and lay eggs in the soil, so treatment must be consistent and rotated between different pesticides. When thrips are found, spray every four days, mostly with a spinosad-based pesticide. Where it is legal, systemic granules (imidacloprid or a similar active ingredient) watered into the soil protect the plant for a month or more; the plant takes the chemical up and pests that bite it die. Do not use systemic granules if spider mites are present: they have been found to speed up spider-mite reproduction rather than kill them, so an infestation can spread faster.
chunks.heading: Thrips: rotate sprays every four days, or use systemic granules

chunks.content: Any premixed potting soil or similar product should be treated for fungus gnats immediately on first use, before an infestation starts. The method: soak Mosquito Bits (the brand) in the water you are about to water with for a few hours, then water with it. This kills the larvae in the soil far more efficiently than the usual published methods like spraying oil on the surface or covering the top of the soil.
chunks.heading: Fungus gnats: treat premixed soil the day you use it

chunks.content: Alocasia tend to attract more pests than other genera. When pests are found on an Alocasia, treat for longer than you would treat a Monstera, and keep watching the plant closely afterward to confirm nothing new has arrived. The pest protocols themselves (thrips, spider mites, mealybugs) are the same as for other aroids.
chunks.heading: Alocasia attract more pests and get treated longer

chunks.content: Cut off the affected leaves immediately, even if it is the plant's only leaf, and spray with a copper fungicide. A fungicide can also be applied while watering. If leaf spot keeps recurring, add more airflow to the setup. Isolate the plant if it sits near other Alocasia, and treat the surrounding plants with a fungicide as well, exactly as you would for a pest outbreak.
chunks.heading: Leaf spot on Alocasia: what to do

answer:
Thrips are tougher to kill than spider mites because they adapt to pesticides fast and lay eggs in the soil, so you need a consistent, rotated treatment rather than a single spray.

When you find thrips, spray every four days, mostly with a spinosad-based pesticide, and rotate between different pesticides rather than using the same one every time. Where it's legal, you can also water systemic granules (imidacloprid or similar) into the soil, which the plant takes up so pests that bite it die, and this protects the plant for a month or more.

One important caution: don't use systemic granules if spider mites are also present. They've been found to speed up spider-mite reproduction instead of killing them, so that can make a spider-mite infestation spread faster.

If these are Alocasia, treat for longer than you would a Monstera, and keep watching closely afterward to make sure nothing new shows up, since Alocasia tend to attract more pests overall. The thrips protocol itself is the same across genera.

queries: leaves turning yellow right after i took them out of the humidity dome, is it light or humidity

chunks.content: Leaves yellowing right after a plant comes out from under the humidity dome are most likely a humidity problem rather than a light problem, usually from taking the dome off too fast. Also make sure the soil is not drying out too much or staying too damp.
chunks.heading: Yellowing leaves once the dome comes off

chunks.content: A plant that seems to be leaning away from the light, or develops a yellowish burned area on the leaf, is getting light burn, the indoor version of sunburn. Fixtures can also run hot, and a leaf touching a hot fixture will burn; it has not happened here but it can.

chunks.content: After planting from tissue culture, leaves sometimes melt away: they turn to mush and die off. This is pretty common. If leaves are turning to mush, consider a slight change to watering, because you might be overwatering, and add some daily airflow if you can. Early in the stage, even opening the dome slightly for a few minutes gets fresh air in.
chunks.heading: Leaves melting away after planting is common

chunks.content: Root rot is the main problem across all genera, especially while plants are small and held in high humidity. The cause is almost always too little airflow under the dome or lid. chunks.content: For the first watering, per half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of a high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. chunks.content: Past the first mix, plants move to a chunky aroid soil: coco coir, perlite, charcoal, coconut husk chips, and a bit of orchid bark. Monstera and Anthurium both love airflow around the roots; Monstera get the chunkiest version, and Anthurium a slightly less chunky one because their roots start thinner. Alocasia and Philodendron get the same ingredients with slightly more fine material and coco coir to hold water, because their finer roots struggle in a mix that is too chunky. chunks.content: The first potting mix for tissue-culture Monstera and Anthurium is tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45 percent each, plus about 10 percent coco coir. For Alocasia and Philodendron it is the same mix with about 20 percent coco coir, with the tree fern and perlite each dropping slightly to make room. The only goal of the change is a bit more dense material for fine roots to pull water from. Any plant with very fine, thin roots gets the denser mix, because fine roots need less airflow and need to be able to grab water from the substrate. A mix that is too dense is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

answer:
For the first potting mix on a tissue-culture Monstera, use tree fern fiber and perlite at about 45 percent each, plus about 10 percent coco coir [general-substrate-water#first-substrate-mix-by-genus].

For the first watering, mix into a half liter of water: one dropper of water-soluble IBA rooting hormone, a very, very small dose of high-phosphorus fertilizer, and Trichoderma harzianum T-22. Water the freshly potted plantlet with that once. The next watering after that gets no fertilizer at all, and light feeding starts with the watering after that. Under a 100 percent humidity dome, it's usually at least ten days before the plant needs water again [general-substrate-water#what-goes-in-the-first-watering].

Once it's acclimated at 75-80 percent humidity and has some size to it (roughly a three-inch pot), a Monstera can move straight to 50 percent humidity without trouble, so you don't need to baby the step-down the way you would with Alocasia [monstera-acclimation#monstera-tolerate-a-faster-humidity-step-down].

chunks.content: Bugs are not common while plantlets are still under the dome, and what to do depends on the bug. Most likely it is springtails or soil mites; if so, leave them, because they are beneficial. A plantlet cannot be sprayed and then put under grow lights: it will most likely burn and die. Spray gently at night so the leaves can dry off.

chunks.content: The grow tents run either AC Infinity S16 light bars, which use Samsung LED diodes and carry light much further down so it dissipates more slowly, or the thicker Barrina TXS45A bars. AC Infinity does not publish PPFD figures, and the S16 can be set to multiple levels, so its output is hard to judge. Its bars use Samsung LM301H EVO LEDs, rated at 3.14 µmol/J PPE, and a set of four IONBEAM S16 bars is listed at 42 watts. The Barrina TXS45A listing (135 W, three 45 W bars, CRI 98) shows, per light and measured at the center of the bar, 429.7 PPFD at 3.94 inches, 216.9 at 7.87 inches, and 137 at 11.81 inches, which is about 2.4 times a Barrina T5 at the same 8-inch distance. A few inches from the plants these fixtures deliver roughly 350 PPFD, which over 12 hours is a DLI of about 15. chunks.content: AC Infinity publishes no PPFD chart for the S16, so its light is estimated from power. A set of four IONBEAM S16 bars draws 42 watts at level 10, and power scales with the level: about 29.4 watts at level 7 and 21 watts at level 5. Multiplying the watts by the LM301H EVO rating of 3.14 µmol/J gives the light the bars put out: about 132 µmol/s at level 10, 92 at level 7, and 66 at level 5. Dividing that by the lit area in square meters gives the average PPFD across the area: over a 2 × 2 ft space (0.37 m²) about 355 at level 10, 248 at level 7, and 177 at level 5; over a 2 × 4 ft space (0.74 m²) about 177, 124, and 89. These are estimates from the LED rating, not measurements, and they are averages across the whole area, while the Barrina charts measure the center of the bar, where light is strongest.

Over a 2×4 ft area, about 177 at level 10, 124 at level 7, 89 at level 5. These are estimates from the LED rating, not actual measurements, and they're averages across the whole lit area [general-light-hardware#estimating-ac-infinity-s16-light-from-its-watts].

For established philodendrons you want at least 250 PPFD, ideally 300+, for 12 to 14 hours a day [general-light#established-plants-at-least-250-ppfd-for-12-to-14-hours]. chunks.heading: When acclimation is done

chunks.content: This is the one temperature rule that matters and most people do not know it: while plantlets are still sealed in the bag or flask, keep them below 75°F. If tissue-culture plantlets are being stored unplanted for a couple of days or longer, they must stay in a cooler spot, because in the bag they melt if it gets too hot. Once they are out of the bag and planted, ordinary room temperatures are fine.
chunks.heading: Unopened bags and flasks must stay below 75°F

chunks.content: When plantlets arrive, do not open the bag. Let them sit sealed for a day or two in the spot where they will be grown, so they adjust to that room's temperature and light before anything else changes.
chunks.heading: Day 0 to day 2: leave them sealed

answer:
Let the plantlets sit sealed in the bag for a day or two first, right in the room where you'll grow them, so they adjust to the temperature and light there. While still sealed in the bag or flask, keep them below 75°F.

Once potted, start humidity at 100 percent under the dome and hold that for at least a week. After about a week, start cracking the vents or lifting the lid slightly and step humidity down slowly from there. Acclimation is finished when the dome or lid can stay off completely and the plant is ready for a bigger pot. In a grow space at 65 to 80 percent ambient humidity, Monstera take about three weeks (18-21 days, sometimes longer) to go from 100 percent down to ambient, Alocasia take four to five weeks, and Anthurium and Philodendron fall in between. A drier room stretches all of these out. Water once at potting, and since it's 100 percent humidity under the dome, they usually won't need water again for at least ten days.

queries: leaves turning yellow right after i took them out of the humidity dome, is it light or humidity

chunks.content: Leaves yellowing right after a plant comes out from under the humidity dome are most likely a humidity problem rather than a light problem, usually from taking the dome off too fast. Also make sure the soil is not drying out too much or staying too damp.
chunks.heading: Yellowing leaves once the dome comes off

chunks.content: A plant that seems to be leaning away from the light, or develops a yellowish burned area on the leaf, is getting light burn, the indoor version of sunburn. Fixtures can also run hot, and a leaf touching a hot fixture will burn; it has not happened here but it can.
chunks.heading: Signs of too much light

chunks.content: After planting from tissue culture, leaves sometimes melt away: they turn to mush and die off. This is pretty common. As long as the base of the plant is fine (the base, not a leaf's stalk), keep taking care of it. If leaves are turning to mush, consider a slight change to watering, because you might be overwatering, and add some daily airflow if you can. Early in the stage, even opening the dome slightly for a few minutes gets fresh air in.
chunks.heading: Leaves melting away after planting is common

chunks.content: Root rot is the main problem across all genera, especially while plants are small and held in high humidity. The cause is almost always too little airflow under the dome or lid. With Alocasia, watch for fungus as well, for the same reason: give them a good amount of airflow. On an established plant, rot looks the same as overwatering: yellowing, wilting, droopiness, browning edges, and mushy sections. Directly after planting from tissue culture the only early sign is usually a loss of firmness, and by the time leaves die it is too late.
chunks.heading: Root rot is the biggest risk for small plants

chunks.content: Water once at potting. Because humidity sits at 100 percent under the dome, it is usually at least ten days before the plantlets need water again.
chunks.heading: Watering cadence under the dome

answer: That's almost always a humidity issue, not light — usually from pulling the dome off too fast. Check that the soil isn't drying out too much or staying too damp, either of those can also cause it.
